blocks.text: On a hot afternoon a continuous welded rail, anchored along its length, cannot grow even though the steel wants to expand by several millimetres per ten metres. The expansion that is not allowed turns into stress, and if that stress is large enough the track buckles sideways into a 'sun kink'.

blocks.markdown: Most materials expand when heated and contract when cooled. For a uniform temperature change $\Delta T$ the **thermal strain** is $\varepsilon_T = \alpha\,\Delta T$, where $\alpha$ is the **coefficient of linear thermal expansion** (units 1/K or 1/$^\circ$C). Thermal strain is a change in size without any stress: a free body expands or contracts and nothing more. Stress appears only when something prevents the free movement.

blocks.title: Thermal strain and thermal elongation
blocks.text: For a member of length $L$ that is free to move, the thermal elongation is $\delta_T=\alpha\,\Delta T\,L$. It is positive for heating. No stress develops in a statically determinate, unrestrained member under uniform temperature change.

blocks.caption: Assumes uniform temperature, linear elastic behaviour, constant $\alpha$ and $E$.

blocks.title: Free expansion of a steel rail
blocks.prompt: A 18 m length of steel rail (alpha = 12e-6 per deg C) is free to expand. It warms from -10 deg C in winter to 40 deg C in summer. Find the change in length.

steps.text: Apply delta = alpha DeltaT L, keeping L in metres.

blocks.answer: The rail lengthens by 10.8 mm, which is why track and bridge decks need expansion gaps.

blocks.caption: Typical values; always use the data supplied in a problem

blocks.markdown: **Restrained expansion.** If a bar is held between rigid walls, the free thermal elongation $\alpha\Delta T L$ is forbidden, so the walls push back with a force $P$ that produces an equal and opposite mechanical shortening $PL/(AE)$. Compatibility says the total change in length is zero: $\alpha \Delta T L - PL/(AE)=0$.

blocks.title: Steel bar between rigid walls
blocks.prompt: A steel bar (E = 200 GPa, alpha = 12e-6 per deg C, A = 800 mm^2) is installed with no stress between two rigid walls and is then heated by 60 deg C. Find the stress and the wall force.

steps.text: Compatibility: thermal elongation equals mechanical compression.
Substitute with E = 200 000 MPa. Length cancels.

blocks.answer: The bar is in 144 MPa compression, with a wall force of 115.2 kN; this is independent of the bar length.

blocks.markdown: **Composite bars.** When two materials with different $\alpha$ are bonded and heated together, each wants to expand by a different amount but they must move together. The material with the larger $\alpha$ is held back (compression) and the other is pulled forward (tension). With no external load the two internal forces are equal and opposite, and compatibility equates the final lengths.

blocks.title: Steel rod inside an aluminium tube
blocks.prompt: A steel rod (E = 200 GPa, alpha = 12e-6, A = 600 mm^2) lies inside an aluminium tube (E = 70 GPa, alpha = 23e-6, A = 1200 mm^2). Both are joined to rigid end plates and the assembly is heated by 50 deg C with no external load. Find the force in each and the stresses.

steps.text: Equilibrium of the end plate with no external load: tension in steel F_s equals compression in aluminium F_a.
Compatibility: final elongations are equal. Aluminium has the larger free expansion, so it is compressed and steel stretched.
Solve for F with A E in newtons: A_s E_s = 1.2e8 N and A_a E_a = 8.4e7 N.

blocks.answer: F is about 27.2 kN: steel is in 45.3 MPa tension and aluminium in 22.6 MPa compression.

blocks.title: Sign and the free-expansion trap
blocks.text: Do not compute the stress from the free elongation of the bar and its length: for a fully restrained bar the length cancels. Also check whether a gap exists; stress arises only from the part of the thermal growth that the supports actually prevent.

points: Thermal strain is alpha x DeltaT and produces elongation alpha DeltaT L with no stress when the member is free.
A fully restrained uniform bar carries stress E alpha DeltaT (compressive on heating), independent of length.
In a bonded two-material member the internal forces are equal and opposite and compatibility equates the final lengths; the higher-alpha material goes into compression on heating.

questions.stem: A straight bar is free to expand and is heated uniformly. Which set of quantities determines its change in length?

options.text: Young's modulus, temperature change and cross-sectional area
Coefficient of expansion, temperature change and original length
Coefficient of expansion, temperature change and cross-sectional area
Young's modulus, coefficient of expansion and applied load

questions.correctOptionText: Coefficient of expansion, temperature change and original length

distractorRationale.a: E and A govern the response to force, not free thermal strain.
distractorRationale.c: Area does not affect thermal strain; length does.
distractorRationale.d: No load is applied to a free bar, and E does not enter delta_T.

questions.explanation: Free thermal elongation is delta = alpha DeltaT L. Neither the modulus nor the area appears because no force is involved.

questions.stem: A uniform bar is installed stress-free between two rigid walls and is then heated. What is the nature of the stress that develops?

options.text: Compressive, and independent of the bar's length
Tensile, and proportional to the bar's length
Compressive, and proportional to the bar's length
Zero, because the bar is uniform

questions.correctOptionText: Compressive, and independent of the bar's length

distractorRationale.a: Correct: sigma = -E alpha DeltaT, length cancels.
distractorRationale.b: Heating pushes against the walls, which is compression, and length cancels.
distractorRationale.c: Right sign but length cancels in the compatibility equation.
distractorRationale.d: Uniformity does not remove restraint; the walls prevent expansion.

questions.explanation: The walls prevent the free expansion, so they push back and the bar is compressed. Since delta_T and the mechanical shortening are both proportional to L, L cancels, leaving sigma = E alpha DeltaT.

questions.stem: A bonded assembly of aluminium (alpha = 23e-6) and steel (alpha = 12e-6) with no external load is heated uniformly. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Aluminium is in tension and steel in compression
Aluminium is in compression and steel in tension
Both remain stress-free because there is no external load

questions.correctOptionText: Aluminium is in compression and steel in tension

distractorRationale.a: Reversed: the material that wants to expand more is held back.
distractorRationale.b: Equilibrium requires one in tension and one in compression when there is no external load.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: aluminium is restrained by the steel and is compressed.
distractorRationale.d: Differential expansion in a bonded assembly causes stress even without loads.

questions.explanation: The aluminium tries to expand more than the steel but is bonded to it, so the steel pulls it back (compression) and the aluminium pulls the steel forward (tension). The forces are equal and opposite.

questions.stem: Two identical-section bars, one steel (E = 200 GPa, alpha = 12e-6) and one aluminium (E = 70 GPa, alpha = 23e-6), are each heated by the same amount while held between rigid walls. Which develops the larger magnitude of stress?

options.text: Steel, because E alpha is larger
They are equal because DeltaT is the same

questions.correctOptionText: Steel, because E alpha is larger

distractorRationale.a: Correct: E alpha = 2.4 MPa/K for steel versus 1.6 MPa/K for aluminium.
distractorRationale.b: Ignores the large difference in stiffness.
distractorRationale.c: Stress depends on material through E alpha.
distractorRationale.d: A smaller E reduces the stress.

questions.explanation: Restrained stress is sigma = E alpha DeltaT. Steel gives 200 000 x 12e-6 = 2.4 MPa per kelvin, aluminium 70 000 x 23e-6 = 1.61 MPa per kelvin.

questions.stem: True or false: a uniform bar fixed at one end only and free at the other, heated uniformly, develops thermal stress.
questions.explanation: The free end can move so the bar expands by alpha DeltaT L without any force. No restraint means no thermal stress.

questions.stem: A copper pipe (alpha = 17e-6 per deg C) is 12 m long and is free to expand. It is heated from 15 deg C to 95 deg C. Find its change in length in mm.
questions.explanation: DeltaT = 80 deg C so delta = 17e-6 x 80 x 12 m = 0.01632 m = 16.32 mm. The pipe is free so no stress arises.

questions.stem: An aluminium rod (E = 70 GPa, alpha = 23e-6 per deg C) is 1.5 m long and fixed at one end. At the other end a gap of 0.6 mm separates it from a rigid wall. The rod is heated by 60 deg C. Find the compressive stress in the rod after it contacts the wall, in MPa.
questions.explanation: Free expansion = 23e-6 x 60 x 1500 = 2.07 mm; the gap absorbs 0.6 mm, so 1.47 mm is prevented. sigma = E x 1.47/1500 = 68.6 MPa compression.

questions.stem: An aluminium bar (E = 70 GPa, alpha = 23e-6 per deg C, A = 900 mm^2) is bonded along its length to a steel bar (E = 200 GPa, alpha = 12e-6 per deg C, A = 300 mm^2) with rigid end plates and no external load. The assembly is heated by 40 deg C. Find the magnitude of the axial force in each bar in kN.
questions.explanation: Forces are equal and opposite. Compatibility gives F[1/(A_aE_a)+1/(A_sE_s)] = (alpha_a - alpha_s) DeltaT = 4.4e-4, with the bracket 3.254e-8 per N, so F = 13.5 kN.

questions.stem: A uniform steel bar is installed stress-free between two rigid walls and is then heated. Derive the thermal stress and explain why it does not depend on the length of the bar.
markingGuide: Notes that the walls prevent the free thermal elongation alpha DeltaT L
States compatibility: total change in length is zero, so thermal elongation equals mechanical shortening PL/(AE)
Explains that L cancels because both effects are proportional to L
States the stress is compressive for heating
questions.explanation: Setting alpha DeltaT L = PL/(AE) gives sigma = P/A = E alpha DeltaT. Every term scales with L, so a longer bar produces more attempted expansion but also more compliance, and the two effects cancel.

questions.stem: Describe how the load shared by two bonded materials of different expansion coefficients is found when the assembly is heated with no external load.
markingGuide: States equilibrium: tension in one material equals compression in the other (F_1 = F_2)
States compatibility: final lengths (thermal plus mechanical) are equal
Writes each member's deformation as alpha DeltaT L plus or minus FL/(AE) with correct signs
Solves for F in terms of (alpha_1 - alpha_2) DeltaT and the compliances
Identifies which material is in tension and which in compression
questions.explanation: With no external load the internal forces balance, so there is one unknown F. Compatibility between thermal and mechanical parts of the deformation supplies the equation that determines it.
